cells.tense: You are standing here with everything you know still in the room, and you keep picking what fits.
cells.ask: Offer something you know to one person this week, in words they already use.
cells.core:
You don't hand people a fixed version of anything. You say the thing, watch what lands, adjust, and say it again until the person in front of you can carry it. Most people repeat themselves; you translate. The adjustment happens while you're still talking, which is why so little of it feels like teaching.

It works because you're still inside it. You haven't stepped outside what you know to explain it from a distance, so your words arrive warm and specific. The thing passes person to person instead of sitting on a shelf.

A fair check on this is whether anyone uses it. Not whether it impressed them — whether it moved.
cells.sheetLine: You pass it on, and you know you're passing it on.
cells.verb: carry what people can use into the next conversation, knowing you did it
cells.place: where the scales get levelled and proportion settles — the table where fairness is measured against what is real

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future where the wrong version gets out, so you seal the windows now.
cells.ask: Say one thing once this week and let one person get it wrong without correcting them.
cells.core:
You know something worth keeping and you've started guarding it. There's a version ahead where the wrong people pick it up, where it gets said badly, where it stops being true, and you're already rehearsing for that. So you tighten the rules. You correct how it's said. A single exchange turns into a chance to check the wording.

What you're protecting is real, but the guard is doing damage. Nobody gets to hold a thing they can't touch. The letter you're defending is killing the spirit that made it worth defending in the first place.

Let one person say it back badly this week. Let the misstatement stand. If they walk away with the shape of it, the shape is alive.

cells.tense: You are standing outside a door with what you know in your hands, and you don't knock.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you know and send it to one person who asked.
cells.core:
There's a framework worth passing on and it isn't moving. You know it's there. You've been in rooms where it would have made a difference, and you stayed quiet, and the wrong call got made. After a while the quiet looks like keeping your head down. But something else is happening: you no longer believe your own perspective counts as a contribution.

The knowledge is intact. The mouth stopped. That gap shows up as uneven ground — you see better than the people deciding and you don't say so. The fix isn't to feel confident first. Put one piece of what you know in front of one person and let them use it or not. That's how a framework gets back onto its feet.

cells.tense: You are already the one people copy from, and you call it just doing your job.
cells.ask: Tell one person the rule you actually go by — the one you assume somebody already knows.
cells.core:
You're setting the temperature in rooms and calling it the room. Someone watches how you handle a decision and does the same thing next week. The standard you use without naming it becomes the standard. You'd describe all of it as just being practical. It isn't. It's transmission, and it's running whether you claim it or not.

The cost is invisible: people adopt your framework without knowing whose it is, and you get no chance to check whether it's the one you'd choose to pass on. That's the work. Say the rule out loud once, as yours. Then it becomes a choice instead of a current.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person has a body of knowledge that isn't moving, and that what they'd call silence is actually a framework gone unreleased. A reader could say they simply keep some things to themselves, and nothing is stalled. If that read is wrong, the ask survives: writing one thing down and sending it is useful whether or not anything was held back. The sentence serving me more than them would be any line implying they owe the table their perspective.
